newsitem.title: IRAN: Iranian sources link wheat buying to livestock use.
newsitem.headline: Iranian sources link wheat buying to livestock use.

text.p: The recent preference of Iranian farmers to use local wheat to feed their livestock, coupled with lower domestic production, has been behind increases in Iranian wheat imports, Iranian wheat industry sources said on Monday.

"There has been some usage of wheat as animal feed because of (low) domestic prices," said one well-placed industry source. "... When it is used like that we have to buy some wheat to take its place."

Iran's government buys wheat from farmers, many of whom also herd sheep, goats and cattle, at prices it sets. It then sells the wheat to bakeries for production of bread which is sold at heavily subsidised retail prices.
The implication is that some farmers have found it more profitable to feed livestock than to sell wheat to the state which has offered less competitive prices, some analysts say.
An Iranian official last month blamed low government purchase prices for sugar beet for a fall in production, forcing the country to import $100 million more sugar in the year to March 1998.
Lower rainfall, which had reduced the local harvest, also helped boost wheat imports, the source added.
"We had limited rain in some areas...there have been dry sections," said the same source, who is active in wheat imports.
Earthquakes in agricultural areas this year have also set back wheat production, limiting supplies to Iran's 60 million people, industry sources said.
The London-based International Grains Council reported earlier in May that Iran had become the world's biggest wheat importer, boosting sales by Australia, Canada and the European Union.
It predicted that Tehran would import 6.6 million tonnes of wheat in the 12 months to June 30, compared to three million tonnes in 1995-1996.
The U.S. Agricultural Department has estimated Iran will import 6.5 million tonnes in 1996-1997.
The source said these estimates had been exaggerated by trade sellers and added that Iran's imports would fluctuate on a monthly basis. He declined to give any actual import figures.
Imports were not a result of re-exports, he added.

European grain traders and officials believe Iran is quietly buying wheat to catch up with rapid growth in its own cities and bake better bread, although trade analysts have suspected that some of Iran's imported wheat is sent on to Central Asia, possibly to Afghanistan.
Kabul flour prices rocketed after Pakistan closed its own border with Afghanistan on March 29 to check wheat shortages.
News that Iran had emerged as the leading wheat importer provoked fierce criticism in the local media.

"Dependence on foreign countries for staple diet in certain cases can even lead to a political crisis in the country, threatening the whole Islamic system," the English-language Tehran Times newspaper said in a May 8 editorial.
"If we are not in a position to fill up the stomachs of our people, we are doomed to face crisis after crisis," it said.
The United Nations Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO) predicts an average Iranian wheat crop of about 10 million tonnes, down two percent from last year.
The new Iranian harvest, mainly grown in the north and west of the country, is just beginning to be stored.
